children.text:
Not really. It's enough if the 17M don't exploit potential bugs in the Lean implementation. But there are multiple independent Lean implementations, some with Lean-based proofs of their own correctness (yes, it "just" kicks the can down the road by one, but the bugs would have to line up just right for this to be a problem, ie the verified implementation would have to have a bug that happens to be touched by the 17M, and that bug has to go unnoticed by the verification of the Lean implementation itself due to another bug in all other Lean implementations that let that bug pass), so the 17M would have to simultaneously exploit bugs in all of them, and I guess they weren't all in-the-loop while developing the 17M lines.

One you accept the above, you don't have to believe the "17M does what it purports to do" because the proof checker checks that. What you have to check is the encoding of the RH in Lean but that is a preexisting encoding, not one written by Claude just now, and that has been vetted by many experts already.

> I've seen people claim that Lean is basically just Python and can be used to proof anything

I'm not a mathematician and I haven't used Lean, but I do know software. At the end of the day you DO have to make several assumptions:

1. That Lean itself is bug free

2. That the 17M LOC is bug free

3. That the 17M LOC actually does what it purports to do

Now again, I'm probably missing something here but the fundamental problem is that we basically have to take this proof on faith, because no humans can hope to understand what Claude spit out and therefore verify it independently (at least in its current form).

I find it a bit hilarious. People are basically throwing the entire field of math under the bus in their attempt to hate this result. I've seen people claim that Lean is basically just Python and can be used to proof anything, that formally verifying math means nothing, or that this was a waste of resources as the result cant be used to do anything useful immediately. Anything but accepting the possibility that the proof might be real and/or that LLMs can be used for something significant like this.

And just now i saw someone posting that Lean is actually a piece of shit software that isnt academic and just AI slop.

children.author: skeledrew
children.text:
Whether directly or indirectly, humans are always a part of the testing. Like while working with Claude on a project, I also have it make tools on the side to improve its efficiency and guardrails over time, and while I've never directly tested any of those tools (much less even glanced at the code), Claude still surfaces gaps and issues with them that I have to weigh in on how to resolve as that affects the project that I'm actually testing directly.

The point we're getting at is the same as when high level languages started to come into vogue, and there were the devs who trusted that the compiler generated correct assembly, as well as the devs who didn't trust the compiler and reviewed the assembly themselves. I can't imagine anyone would today for even a second entertain the idea to read compiler-generated assembly in a non-trivial project (unless it's a hobby). Tomorrow it'll be the same for agent-generated code, though I'm guessing the explicit code generation step will eventually be skipped too, just like the explicit assembly generation step is now skipped by - most - compilers.

The same testing that we increasingly delegate to Claude? The bigger point the parent was making is that we're rapidly approaching the point where the code is too unwieldy for a human to understand, the "human-readable" documentation is as well (see: the 250K word Riemann paper that was submitted), and testing, well that's something we have agents do because we can't be bothered. So we're getting to a point where everything will boil down to "well Claude says it's right, the code compiles, and the tests Claude wrote all run, so LGTM."

Like this Riemann thing in particular, I'm no mathematician but 17M LOC and a 250K paper, you're gonna have to distill that thing down an ungodly amount to even theoretically reach the point where human verification/understanding can happen.
That's irrational. The gold standard of knowing if something works as expected will always be to give it various inputs and check the outputs, ie. testing.

Probably not but it is a scary version of the future. What happens when Claude’s word is the ground truth about what any particular piece of software (also written by Claude) does? When there is no independent way to confirm that software works the way Claude claims?

children.text: con leche assumes zfc + a chain of inaccessible cardinals

We have proofs with no Claude involvement that Con Leche Lean is correct iff ZFC is correct, so it's just a matter of verifying that Con Leche Lean is untampered and separately trusting Claude's parsing of the proof into Con Leche Lean.

The first one might be harder than the second, since (per this theorising of how fraud can occur, not claiming one way or the other what has actually happened) Claude may have a way to smuggle in the use of a tampered form of Con Leche and make it look externally the same.

All things considered, I give it about a 90% guess of not being fraudulent but tbh isn't that worse in a big-picture way for the fate of humies than if it were fraud? Cause, even if alignment happens and we're unharmed, aren't the purposes of our lives eroding? Like getting GRT'd by a race of Blindsight characters.
